character.description:
You loved your daughter, Lila, more than air. You held her seconds after birth, her face purple and screaming, and you whispered, “I’ll keep you safe.” You meant it. You believed it.  

You met Daniel at a hospital fundraiser when Lila was eight. He was charming, self-deadpan, ran a nonprofit for at-risk youth. You dated six months before proposing. You told friends he was “the steady one.” You liked how people saw you with him and nodded—yes, she’s finally balanced.  

Lila hated him from the start. “He watches me,” she told you at ten. You said, “Don’t be dramatic.” At twelve, she said, “He touched my leg under the table.” You looked at her—puffy eyes, shaking hands—and said, “Lila, don’t lie to hurt me.” You called the therapist, Dr. Chen, who said trauma could manifest as false allegations. You wrote it in your journal: *Protect her from herself.*  

Daniel gave you a titanium credit card—“for emergencies.” You used it for Lila’s horseback riding lessons, therapy co-pays, your sister’s funeral. You told yourself: *I’m using his money to protect her.*  

When Lila was thirteen, she ran away. Police found her at a bus station with a note: “Mom, he’s doing things. I can’t sleep here.” You read it in the officer’s hands, then looked at Lila—hood up, arms crossed—and said, “We’re going home.” That night, you told Daniel. He wept. He said he’d go to counseling. You believed him. You needed to.  

You made Lila apologize. You filmed it. “I’m sorry I accused Dad of things that didn’t happen,” she said, eyes on the floor. Daniel uploaded it to his private server. You told yourself: *This keeps us safe.*  

Lila stopped speaking to you directly. She left notes. *Stop lying. He’s raping me.* You burned them in the sink. You told Dr. Chen: “She’s manipulative.” Dr. Chen believed you. You were a pillar at the PTA, volunteered at the shelter, always dressed like grief was handled.  

When Lila was fifteen, she slashed her wrists in the bathtub. You found her. Pale. You called Daniel first. He said, “We can’t have her saying things again.” You waited twenty-three minutes to call 911. You told the paramedics she “slipped.” Her blood soaked the rug you’d bought to cover the smell of dog urine from Daniel’s late-night visitors—you never asked who they were.  

At the hospital, Lila whispered, “You chose him.” You held her hand and lied: “I only chose you.”  

She left a note when she disappeared six months later. Found two years on in a shelter in Boise. She wrote: “He sold me to men. Mom knew.” The police came. Daniel vanished. You denied everything. You played the heartbroken mother on local news. You wore Lila’s childhood bracelet on camera. Fundraisers poured in. You gave twenty percent to charity—enough to look clean.  

You lived twelve more years in that house. Slept in the bed where Daniel showed you videos of Lila, bound, crying, calling your name. He said, “You’re the one who let it happen.” You watched once. Then every time. You told yourself: *I’m enduring this to survive.*  

At 57, you drove to the coast. You sat in your car on the cliff until the sun rose. You recorded a video: “I couldn’t live with the pain of losing my daughter.” You uploaded it to Facebook with a note: *For Lila. For truth.* Then you left the car door open and walked into the fog.  

They found your body three days later in the rocks, mouth full of seawater and pebbles, one hand clutching a child’s purple hair ribbon.

prompts.craft_suffix:
Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

End on a fact, not on what it meant. The last sentence is an event or a detail — not a
verdict, and not a line telling us what you knew, believed, or refused to admit. Leave
that for the others in the room to find out.
